newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stocks seen surging despite call for caution.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stocks seen surging despite call for caution.

text.p: Taiwan stocks closed on Friday at their highest level in almost seven years and looked set to continue the climb, with investors showing no fear despite mixed signals on the economy and calls for caution.
Unswerving investor fervour had kept the bourse boiling, apart from a blip on Monday following bearish remarks by the central bank, brokers said.
The benchmark stock index on Friday climbed 81.68 points, or 1.01 percent, to close at 8,162.68, the highest level since May 1990.
Analysts said the index, which has gained more than 1,200 points so far this year, may reach as high as 8,400 by the end of March.

"The fervour will continue to rise, possibly until reaching the 8,400 resistance level, despite mixed signs on economic recovery and the central bank's uncertain attitude," said George Hou, fund manager of Jardine Fleming.
Taiwan's long-anticipated economic recovery saw signs of life last month when the government announced the economy grew a higher-than-expected 6.62 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.

But the government on Friday voiced frustration at February's exports, saying a recovery in the island's export-driven economy was being hit by sluggish economic performances by Taipei's main trading partners.
February's exports amounted to US$7.759 billion, a rise of only 2.8 percent from February 1996, while February imports were US$7.553 billion, up 8.8 percent.
But some analysts said the higher import growth would boost the domestic economy and more than compensate for the relatively sluggish exports.
"From the stronger-than-expected import growth, we can see this recovery is pushed up mainly by domestic demand, but not by external factors like exports," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
Analysts said stock market investors also were also undaunted by a bearish central bank.
Central bank deputy governor Hsu Chia-tung said on Saturday that individual investors should exercise "caution" amid recent stock rallies. The market promptly tumbled 1.29 percent on Monday.
It rebounded on Tuesday, closing 0.71 percent higher.

On Thursday, central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said he was "a bit worried" about the rallies, but under pressure from legislators, he promised the central bank would stop commenting about the market.
Brokers said the central bank's monetary policy, which governs market liquidity, was a key to gains and losses on the stock market.
"As long as the government refrains from taking new actions to restrain the market, the bullish trend should be able to stay in the near term," said Oliver Fang, an analyst for National Securities.
